paper.title: More than a pinch: a review of pain management during intrauterine device placement.
paper.summary:
PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Pain during intrauterine device (IUD) insertion is currently a major focus of contraceptive care, driven by patient advocacy, social media discourse, and growing recognition that procedural pain may deter patients from seeking an IUD. Concurrently, professional organizations have released updated guidance on pain management during IUD placement. This review summarizes contemporary evidence regarding patient risk factors, procedural techniques, and pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions for IUD insertion pain.
RECENT FINDINGS: Recent literature demonstrates that pain during IUD placement is multifactorial and influenced by patient characteristics, including nulliparity, dysmenorrhea, anxiety, and anticipated pain. Among available interventions, the strongest evidence supports local anesthetic approaches. Ultrasound-guided placement may reduce pain and procedural difficulty. In contrast, routine use of misoprostol is not supported by current evidence. Data regarding non-pharmacologic environmental interventions, oral anxiolytics/opiates, nitrous oxide, intravenous sedation, and operating room-based anesthesia care remain limited or conflicting.
SUMMARY: Effective pain management for IUD placement likely requires a multimodal, patient-centered approach that addresses both physiologic and psychological contributors to pain. Future research should prioritize standardized outcome measures, comparative effectiveness studies, and implementation and cost-effectiveness analyses to inform equitable integration of evidence-based pain management strategies for IUD insertions.

paper.title: Impact of an oral amino acid-containing formulation on clinical and functional outcomes in patients with and without heart failure undergoing cardiac rehabilitation program: a pilot study.
paper.summary:
OBJECTIVES: Skeletal muscle dysfunction and malnutrition are common in patients with cardiovascular disease (CVD), particularly those with heart failure (HF), and may reduce the benefits of cardiac rehabilitation (CR). Amino acid supplementation may enhance exercise-induced adaptations, but evidence during CR remains limited.
METHODS: We conducted a pilot study including 25 patients with CVD, of whom 13 (52 %) had HF, undergoing a 3-month CR program with oral amino acid-containing nutritional formulation. Clinical and nutritional status, quality of life, psychological well-being, physical performance, exercise capacity, laboratory findings, and echocardiographic parameters were assessed at baseline and after 3 months.
RESULTS: Significant improvements were observed in NYHA class, Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form, Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and Short Physical Performance Battery (all p<0.05). Exercise capacity improved, with a mean increase of 59.4 m in the 6-min walk test (p<0.001) and lower Borg scores (p=0.003). NT-proBNP levels decreased (p=0.023). Left ventricular ejection fraction remained unchanged, whereas global longitudinal strain and left atrial volume index improved (p≤0.007).
CONCLUSIONS: Oral amino acid-containing supplementation combined with CR was associated with improved functional capacity, nutritional status, quality of life, and favorable changes in LV myocardial deformation. Larger randomized trials are needed to confirm these findings and determine the incremental contribution of this nutritional formulation.

paper.title: The change in mental well-being over 1 year for people with neurological disabilities and complex needs after moving into individualised housing: an exploratory sequential mixed-methods study.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: Although housing is a social determinant of health, little is known about the well-being of people with a neurological disability after moving into individualised housing from a range of previous living arrangements. This exploratory sequential mixed-methods study explored the change in well-being at 6 and 12 months post-move, addressing the need to better understand well-being trajectories among people with neurological disabilities transitioning to individualised housing.
METHODS: Sixteen participants with a neurological disability completed the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale, and interviews at pre-move, and 6 and 12 months post-move. Paired samples t-test and reliable change index compared Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale scores. A qualitative collective-case study was conducted for three participants with clinically reliable changes of well-being at 12 months.
RESULTS: Well-being significantly increased at 6 months post-move (t(15) = 1.85, P = 0.04), with no significant improvements found at 12 months post-move. The Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-being Scale item of 'feeling useful' significantly increased at 6 months (t(15) = 3.78, P = 0.002) and 12 months post-move (t(15) = 2.42, P = 0.014). Case study analysis revealed an overarching pattern of having a secure base and three sub-patterns: doing more at home, pursuing new opportunities and developing stronger social connections.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings support the transition to individualised housing with results indicating increased feelings of usefulness, an important aspect of well-being. The importance of having a secure base for improved well-being is also highlighted. Further research is needed to understand what sustains well-being in individualised housing.

paper.title: Factors associated with variability in recovery after mild traumatic brain injury among adults referred to outpatient concussion clinics.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: To understand factors associated with symptom and disability recovery trajectories among adults referred to outpatient clinics after mild traumatic brain injury.
METHODS: Adults (n = 110; mean age 39 years, 36% men), were assessed at clinic intake (baseline mean 6.5 weeks), and monthly thereafter for 6 months. Validated questionnaires assessed distress, fear avoidance and catastrophising at baseline, and mild traumatic brain injury symptoms and disability. Using correlations and linear mixed modelling, we explored associations between demographic characteristics (age, gender), baseline psychological factors and recovery as a function of time.
RESULTS: The models predicted improvement in symptoms (R2 = 0.22) and disability (R2 = 0.37). After adjusting for baseline severity of symptoms and disability, higher distress was associated with slower recovery and greater variability for symptoms (P = 0.06) and disability (P < 0.01). Higher baseline catastrophising predicted less symptom improvement (P = 0.02). Those with higher fear avoidance behaviour at baseline showed greater variability in disability outcomes (P = 0.02), even when other psychological variables were accounted for.
CONCLUSIONS: Participants showed improvements on average, in both symptoms and disability. Variability and rates of recovery were associated with distress, catastrophising and fear avoidance. Clinicians can target such psychological factors in treatment and anticipate recovery fluctuations, normalising these while maintaining cautiously optimistic messaging regarding expected good prognosis after mild traumatic brain injury.

paper.title: An experimental study of resilience and its effect on simulated persistent postconcussion symptoms.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a significant public health concern. Several factors contribute to symptom persistence, including potentially modifiable psychological factors. This study focused on resilience as a predictor of simulated persistent postconcussion symptoms (PPCS).
METHODS: Participants were randomly assigned to a mTBI vignette condition with (n = 96) or without resilience-activation (control, n = 95). PPCS was measured using the Rivermead Post-Concussion Symptoms Questionnaire. The potential for a moderated relationship was explored using a measure of emotional distress (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale).
RESULTS: Resilience, as measured by the Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale, was successfully manipulated via the vignette (resilience activation > controls). Hierarchical linear regression (N = 191) demonstrated a significant negative association between group and PPCS, with resilience significantly accounting for 3.27% of unique variance in PPCS. The interaction between predictor variables did not significantly contribute to the overall variance in PPCS.
CONCLUSIONS: Findings are consistent with prior correlational studies of resilience and PPCS, with the present study also isolating a specific role for resilience as distinct from emotional distress. Psychological resilience appears to be a promising target for PPCS reduction.

paper.title: Mild traumatic brain injury recovery: a qualitative study of noise sensitivity, vestibular issues and anxiety interactions.
paper.summary:
BACKGROUND: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a common public health issue, and a substantial minority of individuals experience persistent symptoms that disrupt everyday functioning. Although vestibular symptoms, noise sensitivity and anxiety are each recognised following mTBI, little is known about how people make sense of these symptom experiences or perceive their interaction during recovery.
METHODS: This qualitative study explored the lived experiences of 14 adults recovering from mTBI, purposively sampled from a larger longitudinal cohort. Equal numbers had short (<6 months) or prolonged recovery. Semi-structured interviews were conducted 8-12 months post-injury and analysed using inductive thematic analysis informed by a critical realist framework.
RESULTS: Three themes were identified. 'Noise really hurts' described distressing sensitivity to layered or unexpected noise and strategies to seek quiet. 'Broken spirit level' captured vestibular disturbance, including balance, spatial orientation and visual difficulty. 'Amplified apprehension' reflected heightened anxiety, and avoidance of symptom-provoking activities. Although most participants reported one or more symptoms, a minority explicitly described perceived relationships between them. Noise sensitivity was particularly prominent among those with prolonged recovery.
CONCLUSION: Symptom experiences following mTBI are context dependent and can meaningfully constrain participation. Greater clinical attention to vestibular symptoms, noise sensitivity, and anxiety/fear-avoidance may support more responsive assessment and rehabilitation following mTBI.

paper.title: FGF13 exerts neuroprotective effects via activation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway and serves as a potential biomarker for depression.
paper.summary: Depression is a highly recurrent psychiatric disorder characterized by persistent low mood, anhedonia, and sleep disturbances. The clinical diagnosis of depression currently relies primarily on clinical interviews and standardized assessment scales, lacking objective biological markers. This increases the risk of misdiagnosis and missed diagnosis, while also limiting the precise differentiation of disease subtypes and the individualized prediction of treatment response. Identifying reliable biomarkers has therefore become a major research focus. This study, based on bioinformatics analysis of the GEO database, found that fibroblast growth factor 13 (FGF13) was significantly reduced in the serum of patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). FGF13 belongs to the fibroblast homologous factor (FHF) family and is enriched in neurons of the brain, where it regulates neuronal excitability and synaptic plasticity. However, the role of FGF13 in depression remains unclear. Based on the results of the bioinformatics analysis, experimental validation demonstrated that Fgf13 expression was significantly reduced in corticosterone (CORT)-induced PC12 and SH-SY5Y cells, as well as in the hippocampus of chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) rats, as shown by qRT-PCR and Western blot analyses. Functional experiments demonstrated that FGF13 overexpression enhanced the expression of synaptic plasticity-related proteins (Syn, PSD95, BDNF) and anti-apoptotic protein (Bcl-2), while suppressing pro-apoptotic proteins (Bax, Cleaved-caspase-3) and activating the PI3K/AKT pathway. These effects were markedly reversed by treatment with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. Furthermore, FGF13 overexpression improved neuronal apoptosis and morphological damage in the hippocampus of CUMS rats. Serum ELISA analysis revealed significantly reduced FGF13 levels in patients with depression. Logistic regression analysis showed a negative association between FGF13 expression and depression risk, while ROC analysis demonstrated good diagnostic performance (AUC = 0.936). Collectively, these findings suggest that FGF13 participates in the pathogenesis of depression by regulating synaptic plasticity and neuronal apoptosis and may serve as a promising biomarker and potential therapeutic target.

paper.title: Olfactory dysfunction associated with atopic dermatitis in NC/Tnd mice.
paper.summary: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is one of the intractable chronic inflammatory diseases and is often accompanied by mental disorders, such as depression. On the other hand, depression has been pointed out to be strongly associated with the onset of anosmia. However, no clinical or basic research report has been conducted on whether olfactory dysfunction develops in patients suffering from AD. Since NC/Tnd mice, a spontaneous AD model, exhibit depressive symptoms, NC/Tnd mice were used to clarify this point. We found that mice with AD completely lost their ability to sniff around after exposed to two different kinds of odors and showed reduced expression of both growth-associated protein-43-positive immature olfactory sensory neurons (OSNs) and olfactory marker protein-positive mature OSNs in the olfactory epithelium. Since elevated levels of IL-4, IL-13, and IL-6 in the peripheral blood were detected in NC/Tnd mice with AD, injection of neutralizing mAb against IL-4Rα or IL-6 improved olfactory function and expression of OSNs. Furthermore, administration with signal inhibitors targeting IL-4Rα and IL-6Rβ resulted in the recovery of olfactory function. The present findings suggest that the activation of the IL-4Rα and IL-6Rβ signal pathways by AD suppresses the expression of OSNs in the olfactory epithelium, leading to the loss of smell.

paper.title: System xc- deficiency suppresses microglial glutamate release and inflammation, ameliorating motor dysfunction and anxiety-like behaviors in aged mice.
paper.summary: Elevated extracellular glutamate and neuroinflammation are well-established contributors to aging-related phenotypes. However, the cellular sources of extracellular glutamate and the underlying molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Therefore, this study aimed to determine the role of microglial system xc-, as a candidate source of extracellular glutamate, in physiological brain aging. Using aged xCT knockout (xCTKO) mice, which lack the functional subunit of system xc-, primary microglia, and cultured microglial cells, we examined xCT expression, glutamate release, inflammatory responses, oxidative status, and aging-related behavioral phenotypes. Here, we demonstrate that the microglial system xc- is a major source of pathological extracellular glutamate in the aging mouse brain. Physiological aging, as well as aging-related stimuli significantly increased xCT expression in microglia. Genetic deletion or pharmacological inhibition of xCT significantly attenuated microglial glutamate release, which was enhanced by age-related xCT upregulation. Notably, although TNF-α protein expression was reduced in the brain of aged xCTKO mice compared with that of aged wild-type mice, TNF-α mRNA levels remained elevated. The reduction in TNF-α protein expression was rescued by N-acetyl-l-cysteine, an xCT-independent source of cysteine, suggesting that xCT deficiency suppresses inflammatory cytokine synthesis through reduced intracellular cysteine availability. Furthermore, aged xCTKO mice exhibited improved motor function and reduced anxiety-like behavior without exacerbating oxidative stress or affecting neuronal number. Collectively, these findings identify microglial xCT as an important source of extracellular glutamate during physiological aging and demonstrate that xCT deficiency suppresses microglial glutamate release and neuroinflammation, thereby ameliorating aging-related phenotypes.
